summary: Offers guidance on using the SIP privacy mechanism from RFC 3323, as extended by RFC 3325 and RFC 4244. It clarifies how to handle the affected SIP headers and SDP parameters for each privacy value. This is an informational document, not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Some phone calls should not reveal who you are. This guide explains, step by step, which pieces of information to hide when someone asks for privacy.

questions: what headers should sip privacy hide
subtitle: Clarifying how to hide identity, headers, and session information in phone calls

tldr.problem: The SIP privacy mechanisms defined in RFC 3323 have ambiguities about which headers and parameters should be hidden for each privacy level, leading to interoperability problems.
tldr.mechanism: This document clarifies the recommended handling of each SIP header and SDP parameter for each privacy value (user, header, session, id, history), specifying whether they should be deleted, anonymized, or not added.
tldr.outcome: Implementations can now follow consistent rules when processing privacy requests, improving compatibility and ensuring user privacy is protected consistently.

today: RFC 5379 is an informational document that clarifies RFC 3323. It remains the primary guidance for implementing consistent SIP privacy handling. The clarifications it provides continue to be essential for interoperable privacy services.

sections.title: Privacy Ambiguities in SIP
sections.content:
RFC 3323 defined a privacy mechanism for SIP (Session Initiation Protocol) that lets users request their identity and call details be kept private. However, the original specification left ambiguities about which headers and parameters should actually be hidden for each privacy level. When different implementations interpret these ambiguities differently, interoperability breaks: a privacy service might delete a header that another system expects to see, or fail to hide information that should be private.

This document clarifies those ambiguities by providing concrete, recommended rules for how privacy services should handle each SIP header and SDP (Session Description Protocol) parameter for each of the privacy values: user, header, session, id, and history. It also discusses complications with headers that interact with privacy in complex ways.
sections.plainLanguage: When calling privately, different parts of the phone message need to be hidden in different ways. This document says exactly what to hide and how to hide it so everyone does it the same way.

sections.title: Privacy Values and Roles
sections.content:
The privacy mechanism uses registered priv-values that tell a privacy service what to hide. RFC 3323 defined user, header, session, none, and critical. Later, RFC 3325 added id (for protecting P-Asserted-Identity headers), and RFC 4244 added history (for protecting History-Info headers). A privacy service is a network entity that sits between the caller and the rest of the network, modifying headers and parameters before forwarding the call.

The three main privacy levels work by obscuring different things: user-level privacy hides information the caller inserted (like their name or organization); header-level privacy hides system headers that reveal the caller's path or identity (like Contact, Via, and Record-Route); session-level privacy hides the media session details (IP addresses and ports in the SDP body). The none value means no privacy; critical means the privacy service must apply all requested privacy or fail the request.
sections.plainLanguage: There are different kinds of privacy: hiding your name, hiding which phones touched the call, hiding where the sound comes from. The privacy service is the gatekeeper that does the hiding.

sections.title: Target Headers and Parameters for Each Privacy Level
sections.content:
The core of the guidance is a table showing, for each SIP header and SDP parameter, which ones are targets for each priv-value and what action to take: delete, do not add, or anonymize. The table shown in Section 4.1 specifies behavior for request (R) and response (r) messages.

For user-level privacy, the target headers include Call-ID (which often reveals the caller's IP address), From, In-Reply-To, Organization, Reply-To, Subject, and User-Agent. A privacy service deletes these or instructs user agents not to add them. For header-level privacy (targeting system-level information), the service anonymizes Contact and Via headers with functional alternatives and deletes or strips P-Asserted-Identity, Call-Info, History-Info, and Organization. Session-level privacy targets SDP c, m, o, i, u, e, and p lines, anonymizing them to hide media addresses. The id priv-value targets only P-Asserted-Identity, and history targets only History-Info headers.
sections.plainLanguage: Different privacy levels hide different things: user-level hides stuff you typed, header-level hides routing information, session-level hides the media details. The table tells exactly what to hide for each level.

sections.title: Complex Headers and Interoperability Challenges
sections.content:
Some headers complicate privacy handling because they interact with other mechanisms or serve multiple purposes. Call-ID is essential for dialog matching, so if a privacy service anonymizes it (replacing IP addresses or hostnames with random values), it must retain the original and restore it in messages sent back to the caller. Otherwise, subsequent requests referencing that Call-ID will fail to match.

Similar complications arise with Replaces headers, which contain the Call-ID of a dialog being transferred. If the Call-ID was anonymized upstream, the Replaces header may contain a value that no longer matches the actual dialog ID, causing REFER requests to fail. Record-Route and Via headers can be handled by stripping (removing prior proxies' headers and adding the privacy service's own) or encrypting them, but the privacy service must be able to restore them in responses.

Headers like Identity/Identity-Info are not privacy targets because they provide cryptographic signatures. However, modifying signed headers invalidates the signature, so a privacy service may have to remove these headers entirely if it modifies the From or Call-ID. The document recommends placing the privacy service upstream of the authentication service when possible.
sections.plainLanguage: Some information connects to other information: hiding a phone number might break a message that references that phone number. The guide explains how to handle these tricky cases.

sections.title: Deployment Guidance
sections.content: A privacy service should fail requests with a 500 (Server Error) response if it cannot perform all privacy levels requested, even if the critical priv-value is not present. User agents performing privacy on their own (before sending to the network) follow simpler rules: they anonymize From headers using a canonical anonymous form ('Anonymous' <sip:anonymous@anonymous.invalid>), substitute random values in Call-ID where IP addresses or hostnames appear, and avoid anonymizing Contact and Via unless they can obtain functional anonymous addresses (like through TURN relays or GRUU). The document clarifies that this guidance does not change the privacy mechanism itself but codifies best practices observed through implementation experience.
sections.plainLanguage: Privacy services should either hide everything requested or say no. User phones can do some hiding on their own before sending the call out. The guide makes sure everyone hides the right things.
